summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process

primary_citations.citation_text: Louisiana - Children’s Code Article 601 et seq. (Children’s Code – Child in Need of Care, includes reporting duties)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit held that a child may not be seized from the home absent a court order, parental consent, or exigent circumstances, defined as reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse; the warrantless entry into the home was not justified, though the removal itself was reasonable on those facts.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the elements a Louisiana family must prove to establish a section 1983 unlawful-removal claim in this circuit.
key_cases.quote: there is reasonable cause to believe that the child is in imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse if he remains in his home

key_cases.case_name: Roe v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit held that the plaintiffs raised a fact question whether the caseworker violated the child's Fourth Amendment rights, but reversed on qualified immunity because those rights were not clearly established, while holding the mother had consented to the investigative home visit and that silence cannot supply consent.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the qualified-immunity framework a Louisiana plaintiff must overcome in a section 1983 investigation or search claim.
key_cases.quote: Although they still must obtain the parent's verbal, affirmative consent before conducting an investigative home interview, they need not obtain that consent again when they appear at the parent's doorstep.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that social workers who received and recorded repeated abuse reports but did not remove the child owed him no affirmative substantive-due-process duty of protection, because the harm was inflicted by a private actor and the State had not taken him into custody.
key_cases.relevance: Marks the boundary of the substantive-due-process claim: the constitutional violation in removal cases lies in state action taken, not in state inaction.
key_cases.quote: a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit held the caseworker's entry pursuant to a state removal order objectively reasonable and granted the supervisor immunity, but affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the caseworker for seizing two siblings where, on the plaintiffs' version of the facts, no imminent danger existed.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that Roe and Wooley had already clearly established the imminent-danger requirement, so a caseworker who removes a child without it is not immune.
key_cases.quote: Gates was not required to give social workers fair notice that imminent danger must exist before a child may be removed without a warrant or court order
